title: Judges 5:1–11
context: Judges 5:1–11 opens the Song of Deborah, a victory hymn sung by Deborah and Barak after the defeat of Sisera narrated in chapter 4. The song blesses the LORD because leaders led and the people offered themselves willingly. It recalls the LORD marching from Seir with earthquake and storm, as at Sinai, and describes Israel’s earlier plight, with roads deserted, leadership gone, new gods chosen and no weapons, until Deborah arose as a mother in Israel. Much of the song is old Hebrew poetry with obscure words, so interpreters read some lines tentatively. Arminian and Reformed readers share its central theme: the LORD delivers his people and is praised for it.

verses.text: Then Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam sang on that day, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Deborah and Barak sing on the day of victory. Arminian readers see worship as the right response to deliverance: those whom God used do not claim the glory, but turn the event into public praise of the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the song gives a poetic and theological interpretation of the battle told in prose in chapter 4. Both traditions read the pairing of prose narrative and song as a way Scripture teaches God’s people to remember and interpret his acts.

verses.text: “Because the leaders took the lead in Israel, because the people offered themselves willingly, be blessed, LORD!
verses.arminianNotes: The song blesses the LORD because the leaders led and the people offered themselves willingly. Arminian readers highlight the willing response of God’s people as something the song celebrates, with real human choices playing a part in the deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that willing service is praised and observe that the praise is directed to the LORD, who moved leaders and people to act. Both traditions hold together human willingness and God’s glory here, and the verse itself does not set them against each other.

verses.text: “Hear, you kings! Give ear, you princes! I, even I, will sing to the LORD. I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Deborah calls on kings and princes to listen as she sings to the LORD, the God of Israel. Arminians see the address to foreign rulers as a public witness that Israel’s God is the true deliverer, a message meant to be heard beyond Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the emphatic "I, even I" as personal devotion in the act of praise. Both traditions see the verse as worship that bears witness to the nations about who the LORD is.

verses.text: “LORD, when you went out of Seir, when you marched out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, the sky also dropped. Yes, the clouds dropped water.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD is pictured marching out of Seir and Edom while the earth trembles and the clouds pour rain. Arminian readers read the imagery as the divine warrior coming to help his people, in poetic language similar to Deuteronomy 33:2 and Psalm 68:7–8.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the storm imagery may connect with the battle itself, where the Kishon floods (5:21). Both traditions read the verse as poetic theophany: the LORD’s coming to save is described with the shaking of creation, not as a weather report.

verses.text: The mountains quaked at the LORD’s presence, even Sinai at the presence of the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The mountains quake before the LORD, even Sinai. Arminians see the song linking the victory over Sisera with the LORD’s appearing at Sinai, so that the God who gave the covenant is the God who now defends his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. Translators handle the phrase about Sinai in different ways, and it may be read as a title such as "the One of Sinai." Both traditions read the verse as joining this deliverance to the covenant history begun at Sinai.

verses.text: “In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied. The travelers walked through byways.
verses.arminianNotes: In the days of Shamgar (Judges 3:31) and of Jael, the highways were deserted and travelers used back roads. Arminians read this as a picture of the insecurity of life under oppression, when ordinary trade and travel became dangerous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the irony that Jael, who will be the hero of the song’s ending, is first named here in a time of distress. Both traditions read the verse as historical setting that shows how desperate Israel’s situation had become before God raised up deliverers.

verses.text: The rulers ceased in Israel. They ceased until I, Deborah, arose; Until I arose a mother in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Leadership ceased in Israel until Deborah arose as a mother in Israel. Arminian readers see God raising up an unexpected leader, and they read "mother in Israel" as a title of protective care and leadership for the nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the word translated "rulers" is uncertain and may refer to village life or leaders. Both traditions recognize Deborah’s leadership as God-given in this setting, and readers within each tradition apply that to questions of church leadership in different ways.

verses.text: They chose new gods. Then war was in the gates. Was there a shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: They chose new gods, war came to the gates, and no shield or spear was seen among forty thousand in Israel. Arminians read the line as linking idolatry with Israel’s weakness, the pattern of the book in which turning from the LORD brings oppression.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The Hebrew of the first line is difficult and has been translated in different ways, but the WEB reading fits the cycle of Judges (2:11–15). Both traditions see Israel’s defenselessness as the consequence of covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: My heart is toward the governors of Israel, who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD!
verses.arminianNotes: Deborah’s heart is with the governors of Israel who offered themselves willingly, and she calls the people to bless the LORD. Arminian readers see the song honoring leaders who freely chose to risk themselves for the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and again note the move from honoring human willingness to blessing the LORD. Both traditions read the verse as a model of godly leadership that serves at personal cost and leads others to worship.

verses.text: “Speak, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets, and you who walk by the way.
verses.arminianNotes: Those who ride white donkeys, sit on rich carpets, or walk the road are called to speak. Arminians read the list as covering rich and ordinary people alike, so that every class of Israel shares in telling what God has done.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that white donkeys suggest people of rank. Some words in the line are uncertain in Hebrew. Both traditions read the call as summoning the whole community, from the powerful to the ordinary traveler, to bear witness.

verses.text: Far from the noise of archers, in the places of drawing water, there they will rehearse the LORD’s righteous acts, the righteous acts of his rule in Israel. “Then the LORD’s people went down to the gates.
verses.arminianNotes: At the watering places, away from the archers, people rehearse the LORD’s righteous acts. Arminians see God’s deliverance becoming part of daily conversation, retold where people gather, so that each generation hears it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the LORD’s acts are called "righteous acts," his faithful saving deeds for his people. Both traditions see the verse teaching that remembering and retelling God’s works is central to the life of his people.
